subject: english-literature
title: Larkin's Provincial Lyric: The Movement and After
welcome_lead: Examine Philip Larkin's post-war lyric mode — provincial, ironic, formally restrained — and his place in the Movement.
meta_desc: A-Level Edexcel Poetry Options adventure on Philip Larkin: The Movement, provincial lyric, irony, and post-war England.
final_note: Larkin's plainness is a discipline, not an absence. Behind the casual diction lies a poet who counts every syllable.

concepts.def: A loose 1950s grouping of British poets (Larkin, Amis, Davie, Gunn, Enright) rejecting modernist obscurity in favour of clarity and metre.
Larkin's distinctive register — Hull-based, demotic, deflationary — as a corrective to metropolitan and modernist excess.
Larkin's preferred form: rhymed quatrains with subtle metrical variation, reanimating traditional lyric for post-war Britain.
Larkin's characteristic move: building lyric expectation, then deflating it (e.g. 'Mr Bleaney', 'Church Going').
Many Larkin poems chart post-war social mobility, class anxiety, and the bureaucratisation of intimacy.
Larkin's mature collections: The Less Deceived (1955), The Whitsun Weddings (1964), High Windows (1974).

walkthroughs.body_html: The Movement was named by J.D. Scott in The Spectator (October 1954). Robert Conquest's New Lines (1956) anthologised its members: Larkin, Kingsley Amis, Donald Davie, Thom Gunn, D.J. Enright, John Wain, Elizabeth Jennings, Robert Conquest. They rejected what they saw as modernist obscurity and neo-Romantic excess (Dylan Thomas) in favour of metrical clarity, ironic tone, and provincial setting. Critics including Blake Morrison detail their formal conservatism as ideological.

The title poem comprises eight ten-line stanzas, rhymed ABABCDECDE, in loose iambic pentameter with one trimeter line per stanza. The journey from Hull to London frames an accumulating witness of wedding parties on platforms. Critics including Andrew Motion and James Booth note the poem's movement from detached irony to qualified affirmation — the closing 'arrow-shower / Sent out of sight, somewhere becoming rain' is Larkin at his most lyrically open.

Andrew Motion's 1993 biography and the 1992 publication of Larkin's Selected Letters revealed misogynistic, racist private views that complicated readings of the poems. Critics including Lisa Jardine and Tom Paulin demanded reassessment; defenders including James Booth argued the poems exceed the man. AQA/Edexcel responses benefit from acknowledging this contested reception while attending closely to the poems.
